tagline: Forest roads and river valleys connect a bridge wreck and lumber country
intro: Route 6 crosses forested hills, farmland and river valleys in Pennsylvania’s northern tier. The state scenic byway covers 211 miles in Warren, McKean, Potter and Tioga counties, including extensions and offsets of U.S. 6. The PA Route 6 Alliance says the corridor meets all six byway criteria: historic, cultural, recreational, natural, archaeological and scenic. Within that landscape, the highway winds through mountainous terrain south of Warren and descends Denton Hill before reaching the Lumber Museum and the Pine Creek valley.

When U.S. 6 was approved in 1926, its western end was Kane; by the end of 1927, it extended west to Erie. The modern byway designation followed years of work led by the PA Route 6 Alliance. All 34 municipalities passed supporting resolutions, and the designation was celebrated in Coudersport on October 30, 2025.

From Warren, the road winds south into the Allegheny National Forest through Clarendon to Sheffield, then turns east toward Kane and Mount Jewett. Beyond Smethport and Port Allegany comes Coudersport, followed by the climb over Denton Hill. The road then follows Pine Creek through Galeton toward Ansonia, where the creek turns south into its gorge. U.S. 6 continues through Wellsboro toward Mansfield.

moments.title: Kinzua Bridge
moments.text: Kinzua’s fallen towers remain where the 2003 tornado left them. The storm destroyed 11 of the viaduct’s 20 spans, ending the crossing over Kinzua Creek. The bridge lost that day was the 1900 structure, which had replaced the original 1882 bridge. In 2011, the remaining support towers became the basis for a different kind of crossing: a pedestrian skywalk extending 600 feet into the gorge. Its end platform includes glass through which visitors could look down. Excursion trains had stopped using the bridge in June 2002, when it closed for restoration, a year before the storm.

moments.title: Pennsylvania Lumber Museum
moments.text: Logging locomotives and sawmill equipment give Pennsylvania’s lumber industry a material scale at this museum near Galeton. Replica buildings explain industrial processes and loggers’ lives during the late-1800s logging boom. One cabin has a different provenance: forester Bob Webber lived in it in Pine Creek Gorge. After his death in 2015, it was moved intact to the museum. Webber developed hiking trails in Tiadaghton State Forest, and hikers and history enthusiasts campaigned to preserve his home. The collection addresses both the industry’s economic importance and the ecological destruction that accompanied logging, linking its machines to their consequences.

moments.title: Ansonia
moments.text: At Ansonia, Pine Creek leaves U.S. 6 and turns south into its gorge. It once flowed northeast. About 20,000 years ago, debris from the receding Laurentide Continental Glacier blocked that course. Meltwater formed a lake near present-day Ansonia; when it overflowed the debris dam, the creek flooded south and cut a deep channel toward the West Branch Susquehanna River. Marsh Creek joins Pine Creek here, and the Pine Creek Rail Trail has an access area in the community. The rail trail follows a former New York Central railroad bed, adding another way through the valley shaped by that change of course.
